title: Manufacturable, damage-tolerant bulk metallic glasses

concept.text: The innovation would be a reliable way to manufacture large, useful metal components that retain a substantially amorphous atomic structure and tolerate damage during service. In a metallic glass, atoms lack the repeating crystal arrangement found in conventional metals. Bulk metallic glasses already exist; the proposed advance is to combine practical component dimensions, controlled manufacturing and dependable mechanical behavior in an integrated production capability.

Two linked problems define the concept. The alloy and its cooling conditions must prevent crystallization throughout the component, including its interior. The resulting glass must also resist catastrophic fracture: deformation can concentrate in narrow shear bands instead of spreading through the material. Damage tolerance therefore means more than successfully producing an amorphous part. Low tensile ductility and high fracture toughness can coexist in some compositions; the ability to stretch before breaking and the resistance to crack growth are distinct properties.

Proposed scope: success should be defined for useful alloy families and specified applications. It need not require arbitrary compositions, perfect material, or the complete elimination of processing gradients. Permissible imperfections and structural variation should instead be bounded by demonstrated component performance.

significance.text: Metallic glasses offer combinations of high strength, a large elastic limit and thermoplastic formability that motivate structural and precision-manufacturing applications. A process that preserves these useful properties in larger components while delivering reliable fracture behavior could expand the range of viable parts. The supplied review identifies precision gears and aerospace applications as relevant opportunities, while emphasizing that fracture toughness must be dependable for commercialization.

The potentially revolutionary step is the combination of manufacturability and mechanical reliability. Overcoming section-size restrictions would make more geometries accessible; controlling fracture behavior would make their service performance more predictable. Neither improvement alone establishes the full capability. A large amorphous casting that fails unpredictably, or a tough laboratory specimen that cannot be reproduced at useful dimensions, leaves a central barrier unresolved.

Conditional downstream synthesis: qualified production could support broader use of metallic glasses in load-bearing and precision-formed components, provided yield, assembly and economics are competitive. This would not establish universal superiority over crystalline alloys. Amorphous structure alone does not guarantee exceptional corrosion resistance, tensile toughness or commercial adoption. No historical benchmark comparison was supplied, so the significance rests on the capability gained rather than a demonstrated ranking against past metallurgy breakthroughs.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing integrated capability, as framed by the supplied evidence, is reproducible production of industrially relevant bulk metallic-glass parts with reliably qualified damage tolerance. Glass-forming ability constrains which compositions can remain amorphous and the cooling conditions they require. Increasing section thickness makes it harder to maintain the conditions needed to avoid crystallization throughout the part. Alloy selection, processing and component geometry therefore have to be solved together.

The mechanical barrier is controlling deformation and fracture despite shear localization. The review connects strain softening and rapidly propagating shear bands with catastrophic failure, and identifies process-related variation in fracture toughness as an ongoing issue in its 2022 account. Some compositions are highly tough, so the challenge cannot be reduced to making every metallic glass intrinsically brittle or ductile. It requires understanding and controlling the conditions under which a particular material fails predictably and without abrupt catastrophic loss.

Fracture behavior depends on composition, processing, temperature, specimen size and geometry. A favorable result in one specimen or loading condition consequently does not establish component-wide reliability. Engineering development must connect processing history and material structure to behavior under the intended service conditions, while preserving useful glass-forming and shaping characteristics.

Proposed engineering extension: an industrial solution must also accommodate fatigue, corrosion exposure, joining or assembly, production variability and cost. These are application-qualification barriers included in this concept's scope; the supplied review does not establish that each has been solved or prescribe numerical acceptance thresholds.

current_state.text: Wook Ha Ryu, Ji Young Kim and Eun Soo Park published “Toward damage-tolerant bulk metallic glasses: Fracture behavior and brittle–ductile transition” on 30 August 2022, DOI 10.1557/s43577-022-00370-x. The review describes existing bulk metallic glasses, advances in glass-forming ability, manufacturing size restrictions and fracture limitations. This establishes an existing materials field with substantial progress; the hypothetical innovation is the stronger integrated manufacturing and service-reliability capability.

The authors characterize tensile ductility as generally close to zero and explain its connection to localized deformation. They also discuss brittle–ductile transitions and compositions with high fracture toughness. These observations are compatible: resistance to crack growth is different from the amount of uniform tensile deformation a specimen can sustain. The evidence therefore does not justify treating every bulk metallic glass as having low fracture toughness, nor does a tough composition establish broad tensile ductility.

The review identifies manufacturing restrictions, brittle fracture and processing-related variations in key properties as obstacles to commercialization. It does not demonstrate an industrial process meeting the combined criteria proposed here for large parts, through-thickness amorphous structure and reliable service qualification. The supplied material provides no verified component dimensions, production yields or numerical toughness and fatigue results sufficient to quantify such an integrated achievement.

Evidence boundary: the supplied review assessment reports identity-verified, complete HTML and PDF article text with no extraction issues or truncation; its conclusions do not depend on inspecting figure images. Those reported text findings support the account above. However, the supplied freshness search record is empty. Developments after the 2022 review, including whether the integrated capability remained unmet on 1 November 2026, cannot be determined from these inputs. This gap does not invalidate the review or prove that later demonstrations do not exist.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independent producers should manufacture industrially relevant large components in more than one practical composition, with a substantially amorphous structure verified through the full thickness. The intended application should determine component dimensions, acceptable crystalline content, permissible defects and gradients, and the required consistency between batches. These are proposed criteria, not established standards or achievements reported by the source.
completion_criteria.label: Independent producers make large amorphous components in multiple practical compositions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed mechanical qualification: representative components should meet predefined requirements for fracture toughness, tensile behavior, fatigue and relevant environmental exposure. Testing should address the intended temperature range, geometry, loading conditions and credible damage states. Toughness and tensile ductility should be reported separately, and favorable average performance should be accompanied by evidence that variability and failure modes remain within the application's acceptable bounds.
completion_criteria.label: Components meet mechanical and environmental requirements with acceptable failure variability

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: separate production campaigns and independent verification should reproduce both structure and performance. Production yield, joining or assembly methods and cost should support a substantial real application. A convincing demonstration should identify where the process works and where it fails, including composition, thickness and service-condition limits. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, not universal manufacturability or damage tolerance.
completion_criteria.label: Independent campaigns reproduce structure and performance within documented practical limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MET-01, “Predictive metallurgy from composition to lifetime,” overlaps through the need to connect alloy chemistry and processing with structure, fracture behavior and service life. Predictive tools could help design and qualify bulk metallic glasses, but MET-07 requires a demonstrated manufacturing capability and dependable physical components; prediction alone would not complete it.

Roster-based synthesis: MET-04, “Structural metals that repeatedly heal fatigue damage in service,” shares the goal of reliable service under damage. MET-07 concerns controlling deformation and fracture in manufactured metallic-glass parts; it does not require damage to heal after it forms. MET-08, “Practical room-temperature superplastic forming of common alloys,” overlaps in shaping complex metal parts, but thermoplastic formability in metallic glasses is distinct from room-temperature superplasticity in common alloys.

Roster-based synthesis: MET-11, “Structural alloys with broadly reliable intrinsic corrosion resistance,” intersects with the environmental qualification of metallic-glass components. Corrosion resistance remains a separate performance requirement rather than an automatic consequence of glass formation. MET-06, “A practical structural alloy system for sustained fusion-reactor conditions,” and MET-09, “Uncoated structural alloys for very high temperatures in oxidizing environments,” address demanding service environments that would require additional qualification beyond demonstrating MET-07.

Roster-based synthesis: MET-02, “Steel from ore without fossil carbon at competitive global scale,” MET-03, “Repeated, high-grade recycling of mixed steel scrap,” and MET-10, “Repeated upcycling of mixed aluminum scrap into demanding alloys,” concern production routes or recovery of useful material from feedstocks. They may share concerns about processing control and economics, but MET-07 specifically targets amorphous structure and damage-tolerant components. None of these capabilities implies the others.

Roster-based synthesis: MET-05, “Titanium at mass-market structural-metal cost,” shares the ambition of making an attractive material practical at scale. Its central target is titanium cost; MET-07 requires glass formation and reliable mechanical behavior alongside viable manufacturing economics. Success in one would not establish success in the other.

brief.title: Large metal parts that resist sudden fracture
possible: Manufacturers could make larger precision gears and aerospace parts from metallic glass: metal whose atoms lack the repeating arrangement of ordinary metals. These parts would retain that structure throughout their thickness and tolerate damage reliably in service.
why: Metallic glasses combine high strength with an ability to spring back after deformation and soften for shaping when heated. Reliable production of larger parts could bring those properties to more load-bearing components and precision shapes.

sources.who: Wook Ha Ryu, Ji Young Kim and Eun Soo Park
sources.showed: Their review describes metallic glasses that resist crack growth despite barely stretching before breaking. It also identifies manufacturing size limits and variation in fracture behavior.
sources.quote:
BMGs whose fracture toughness is similar
to those of the toughest engineering alloys such as low-carbon
steel and Ti alloys have been reported in Zr-based and Pd-
based alloy systems.
sources.cited_for: Resistance to crack growth and the ability to stretch before breaking are distinct properties.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate reproducible manufacture of large components with dependable performance in service.

sources.who: Yiyu Shen, Yingqi Li, Chen Chen and Hai-Lung Tsai
sources.showed: The team built complex metallic-glass structures by laser welding thin metal sheets together. Selected manufacturing settings preserved the disordered atomic structure.
sources.quote:
In this study, 3D, large dimensions of amorphous 
structures with complex geometry are manufactured by our newly developed Laser  Foil Printing 
(LFP) technology.
sources.cited_for: Building parts from thin sheets offers a route beyond the shape and thickness limits of casting.
sources.not_established: Preserving the glass structure does not establish resistance to fracture or reliable production across different metal mixtures.

sources.who: Yuqiao Zeng, Nobuyuki Nishiyama, Tokujiro Yamamoto and Akihisa Inoue
sources.showed: The team made nickel-rich metallic-glass rods reaching 21 mm in diameter. Samples deformed permanently under compression but failed abruptly when pulled.
sources.quote:
The samples exhibit an elastic
deformation followed by a catastrophic failure.
sources.cited_for: Larger glassy rods and deformation under compression do not establish safe behavior under tension.
sources.not_established: The work does not demonstrate damage-tolerant components under the range of conditions required in service.

sources.showed: The team made a palladium-based metallic glass with high resistance to crack growth. Its ability to stretch permanently before breaking remained small.
sources.quote:
Interestingly, a small total
plastic strain of∼0.15% was recorded.
sources.cited_for: A metallic glass can strongly resist crack growth without stretching much before failure.
sources.not_established: A tough laboratory material does not establish large components, reproducible production or dependable service performance.

shown: Researchers have demonstrated important pieces separately: Shen and colleagues printed complex glassy structures, Zeng and colleagues cast thick rods, and Demetriou and colleagues made a glass that strongly resists crack growth.
missing: Reproducible manufacture of useful large parts that retain a mostly disordered atomic structure throughout their thickness remains to be demonstrated.
Representative components still need dependable fracture, repeated-loading and environmental performance across intended service conditions.
Independent production runs still need to reproduce those results with practical assembly methods, production yield and cost.

milestones.label: Independent producers make large glassy parts in multiple metal mixtures
milestones.explanation: Independent producers would have to make useful large parts in multiple metal mixtures, retaining a mostly disordered structure throughout. This would establish that manufacturing extends beyond isolated specimens.

milestones.label: Components meet service requirements with predictable failure behavior
milestones.explanation: Components would have to meet requirements for cracking, stretching, repeated loading and environmental exposure, with acceptable variation. This would establish dependable behavior under intended service conditions.

milestones.label: Independent production runs reproduce practical parts and performance
milestones.explanation: Separate production runs and independent checks would have to reproduce structure and performance within stated limits, with workable yield, assembly and cost. This would establish a practical capability for a substantial application.

uncertain: The target applications and metal mixtures remain undecided, leaving useful dimensions and acceptable structural imperfections undefined.
Required mechanical performance, environmental resistance and acceptable production variation still depend on the application.
How widely results from particular specimens extend across component shapes, temperatures and loading conditions remains uncertain.

page.title: Damage-tolerant bulk metallic glass components
page.definition: Bulk metallic glass (BMG) components retain an atomic structure without a repeating crystal lattice and meet a specified application's requirements for dimensions, strength, crack resistance and service life. Bulk denotes section thickness above about 1 mm; qualification covers manufacturing variation.

goal.need: A 2022 review reports fracture toughness of 1–230 MPa·m^(1/2) across BMG compositions and identifies process-related variation as a commercialization barrier. NASA's gear programme seeks heater-free cryogenic actuation; its Curiosity-type rover estimates quantify one application's energy and mass benefits. Fracture resistance must survive the transition from laboratory specimens to manufactured components.

figures.caption: Estimated savings from removing gearbox heaters from a Curiosity-type rover.
figures.note: Application estimates published in 2019, not measured mission savings.

statements.body: NASA Game Changing Development programme, Bulk Metallic Glass Gears project
statements.quote: The BMG Gears project seeks to advance the technology to a technology readiness level (TRL) of six
statements.context: The stated application is cryogenic planetary gearboxes.

statements.quote: The final product needs to meet the performance specifications provided by the Customer
statements.context: The report addresses acceptance of BMG feedstock and qualification of spacecraft gear castings.

statements.body: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, COLDArm gearmotor developers
statements.quote: assess manufacturing variability and establish design allowables for mechanical properties.
statements.context: The passage describes an activity accompanying gearmotor qualification, after tooth fractures were found following extended life testing.

completion.title: A production BMG component passes its application's damage-tolerance qualification and acceptance tests.
completion.criterion: For one named alloy, manufacturing route and component geometry, production parts pass the application's published qualification and lot-acceptance requirements for amorphous structure, flaw tolerance and service life at specified temperatures and loads. Mechanical acceptance uses design allowables established for manufacturing variability. Dimensions, defect limits and mechanical thresholds belong to that application's specification.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no combined external completion threshold was located.
completion.basis: Searched NASA's BMG gear targets and qualification roadmap, ASTM E399/E1820 and DARPA Structural Amorphous Metals targets; no combined production and damage-tolerance acceptance test was found. This fallback follows NASA's customer-specification approach and its identified need for manufacturing-based mechanical allowables. It concerns one accepted component design; the opened sources do not establish that this full test has been met.

milestones.title: A metallic glass is produced with a section thickness greater than about 1 mm.
milestones.criterion: Make an amorphous metallic specimen with section thickness greater than about 1 mm, the bulk convention. Nickel-based result: Ni50Pd30P20 was formed as a 21 mm-diameter rod, reported on 1 October 2009. Palladium-based result: Pd79Ag3.5P6Si9.5Ge2 formed glassy rods 6 mm in diameter, reported on 9 January 2011. Neither opened account supplies a production-run sample count.
milestones.set_by: The metallic-glass community's bulk-size convention, explicitly described by NASA/JPL in 2016.

milestones.title: A bulk metallic glass sustains stable crack growth with increasing crack resistance.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate stable extension under mode I, or crack-opening, loading with a rising crack-resistance curve. Palladium-based result: Demetriou et al. used 2.1 × 2.1 × 20 mm micronotched bending beams of Pd79Ag3.5P6Si9.5Ge2 and observed stable growth over hundreds of micrometres. Crack-opening-displacement analysis gave near-steady-state KJc ≈200 MPa·m^(1/2); this was not a plane-strain KIc measurement. Published on 9 January 2011; specimen count is not stated in the opened main text.
milestones.set_by: Fracture-mechanics convention identifying rising crack resistance and stable extension, applied to a palladium-based BMG by Demetriou et al.; no universal numerical toughness cutoff is implied.
milestones.threshold_quote: The glass demonstrates extensive rising R-curve behaviour indicative of stable crack growth over hundreds of micrometres.

milestones.title: Each production feedstock lot yields fully amorphous, fully formed acceptance castings.
milestones.criterion: Each remelt-stock lot produces fully amorphous, fully formed, low-defect acceptance castings in reference dies reproducing the component's processing characteristics. NASA's recommendation gives no universal numerical defect limit. Zirconium-based result: the 2024 gearmotor report describes injection-moulded gears, with fabrication then limited to <100 g including gates and runners and approximately 5 mm critical casting thickness. It supplies no lot-acceptance counts.
milestones.set_by: NASA Langley, NASA/TP–2018-220246, sections 2.2 and 3.2; this recommendation was written for cast S77PT spacecraft gear material.

milestones.title: A BMG prototype operates under its intended critical environmental conditions.
milestones.criterion: A high fidelity component or system prototype addresses critical scaling and operates in the relevant environment, NASA's TRL 6 hardware criterion. Zirconium-based result: one cryogenic engineering unit ran 1.5 million motor revolutions under vacuum at ≤−180 °C, 1 N·m output torque and 2000 rpm input, reversing every 2000 input revolutions. Testing ended with motor stalling. This is a 2024 conference report.
milestones.set_by: NASA's Technology Readiness Levels table, hardware row 6; the criterion is stated in a table. The BMG Gears programme explicitly targeted this level for cryogenic gears.

milestones.title: A finished BMG component passes qualification for its intended operational environment.
milestones.criterion: The final product in its final configuration demonstrates performance through test and analysis for its intended operational environment and platform, NASA's TRL 8 hardware criterion. Zirconium-based result: one COLDArm gearmotor qualification unit passed three times its Table 3 duty profile at assumed ambient 25 °C, −180 °C and −100 °C. Approximately 5,269,000 total motor revolutions included extended testing; subsequent inspection found gear-tooth fractures. The 2024 report establishes design life qualification without assigning an overall TRL 8.
milestones.set_by: NASA's Technology Readiness Levels table, hardware row 8; the criterion is stated in a table. This is a generic qualification framework, not a published BMG programme target.

not_found: Public lot-acceptance datasets and manufacturing-based damage-tolerance allowables were not found for the cited COLDArm gearmotors.
Comparable prototype and operational qualification reports were not found for palladium- or nickel-based BMG components.
The supplied OSTI laser-foil-printing paper could not be reopened.
The publisher page for Fu et al.'s industrial-casting paper, DOI 10.1016/j.actamat.2026.122744, could not be opened.

results.finding: One laser-printed LM105 metallic-glass cube had a 10 mm section thickness.
results.detail: XRD at sampled locations detected no crystalline phase above its approximately 2% detection limit; DSC and hardness results also supported the amorphous finding.
results.quote:
A fully amorphous 10-mm cubic sample was successful ly built by spot-welding as shown in 
Fig. 4, and the same parameters were used to constr uct several large 3D MG parts as shown in 
Fig. 9.

results.finding: Ni50Pd30P20 glassy rod, sample count not stated, formed with a diameter of 21 mm.
results.detail: The rod was prepared by water quenching with repeated flux treatment; X-ray diffraction and calorimetry supported its glassy structure.
results.quote:
The alloys with Pd contents higher than 25 at% exhibit high glass-forming ability, as is evidenced from the formation of a
cylindrical Ni50Pd30P20 glassy rod with a diameter of 21 mm.

results.finding: Pd79Ag3.5P6Si9.5Ge2 glassy rods reached 6 mm diameter; sample count not stated.
results.detail: X-ray diffraction, microscopy and calorimetry were used to verify the amorphous structure.
results.quote:
Specifically, alloy
Pd79Ag3.5P6Si9.5Ge2 was found capable of forming glassy rods
6 mm in diameter.

results.finding: Pd79Ag3.5P6Si9.5Ge2 beams showed stable crack growth over hundreds of micrometres; sample count not stated.
results.detail: Mode I bending tests showed a rising resistance curve. The near-steady-state toughness was derived using crack-tip opening displacement, not measured as plane-strain KIc.
results.quote:
The glass
demonstrates extensive risingR-curve behaviour indicative of stable
crack growth over hundreds of micrometres.

results.finding: Pd40Cu30Ni10P20 amorphous cylinders, sample count not stated, reached 72 mm in diameter.
results.detail: The molten alloy underwent flux treatment before production. The abstract reports cylinders ranging from 50 to 72 mm in diameter.
results.quote: The use of the molten Pd–Cu–Ni–P alloy subjected to the flux treatment enabled the production of bulk amorphous alloys in cylindrical forms of 50 to 72 mm in diameter and 52 to 75 mm in length.

results.finding: Ni60Pd20P14Si2B4 metallic glass: sample count not stated; achievable processing diameter 25 mm.
results.quote: The enhanced GFA results in the largest achievable processing diameter (25 mm) of Ni-based bulk metallic glasses, which is more than four times larger than that of Ni60Pd20P20.

results.finding: Three Pd77.5Cu6Si16.5 specimens showed rising crack resistance over approximately 500 µm of crack extension.
results.detail: In situ three-point bending tests produced estimated crack-growth toughness of approximately 250–400 MPa·m½. The authors caution that the results are sample-size and likely geometry-dependent, and discuss uncertainty in J–K conversion.
results.quote:
Additional
in situ tests on the smaller-sized samples in a scanning electron microscope revealed stable crack growth
and progressive resistance to crack extension, i.e., rising crack-resistance ( R-curve) behavior.

results.finding: Pd77.5Cu6Si16.5 amorphous rods were produced at 8 mm diameter; rod count was not reported.
results.detail: The authors verified the amorphous structure using X-ray diffraction.
results.quote:
water-quenched from 1 150/C14C to obtain amorphous rods of 8 mm
diameter.

results.finding: Zr61Ti2Cu25Al12 bulk metallic glass: R-curve obtained; specimen count and numerical crack-resistance values not stated.
results.detail: Fatigue-precracked samples were tested using single- and multiple-specimen techniques. The text does not state that the curve rises, that crack extension was stable, or that loading was mode I.
results.quote: The crack-resistance curve (R-curve) of this BMG has been obtained from fatigue pre-crack samples, employing standard "single- specimen" and "multiple-specimen" techniques.
